analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before intelligence agencies search communications of Americans, and bans law enforcement buying data from brokers.
analysis.headline: The Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2026 was introduced on March 12, 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require a court order before federal intelligence agencies can search communications of Americans collected under the FISA 702 program, ban "reverse targeting" of people in the U.S., limit how long agencies can keep data on Americans, and bar federal law enforcement from buying Americans' location, biometric, and browsing data from commercial data brokers. It would also add warrant protection for car data and web browsing records, and give independent privacy advocates a bigger role at the secret surveillance court. To get that done, it extends the underlying 702 surveillance authority for four more years, to April 2030.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose phone calls, emails, and location data get swept up when the government collects foreign communications. Nearly every American has communications in the 702 database. The bill would stop federal agents from searching that database without a warrant, stop agencies from collecting communications of people inside the U.S. directly, stop them from buying personal data from brokers to dodge warrant requirements, and make the secret surveillance court more adversarial by appointing privacy and technical experts to argue against government applications. Tech and telecom companies also gain clearer limits on when the government can compel their assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans swept into surveillance databases

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal officers from searching information collected under FISA Section 702 using an American's identity without a warrant or court order, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, consent, and defensive cybersecurity, and creates an audit record system for every query [S2].

Bans "reverse targeting" — using foreign surveillance authority as a pretext to collect the communications of a specific, known person inside the U.S. — and prohibits warrantless acquisition of domestic communications outright [S2].

Adds Title II, the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act, which bars federal law enforcement agencies from obtaining Americans' personal data — including location, biometric, and web browsing data — from data brokers in exchange for anything of value, closes the door on getting it through other government agencies, and blocks such illegally obtained data from use as evidence [S2].

Requires a warrant or court order for any government targeting of a person inside the U.S. that collects communications content, location information, browsing history, or search history, replacing several broader FISA collection authorities [S2].

Requires privacy, civil-liberties, and technical experts (amici curiae) to be appointed in most significant surveillance court proceedings, gives them the power to appeal legal questions to higher courts, and expands declassification of major surveillance court decisions [S2].

Limits how long agencies may keep information about Americans collected under 702 — generally destroying it within five years of collection — and repeals the expanded definition of "electronic communication service provider" that pulled smaller tech companies into compulsion [S2].

Adds warrant protections for web browsing records, search queries, and location information under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, protects car data from warrantless federal searches, and requires state and local police using federal grants to report publicly on data broker purchases [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community — FBI, NSA, and other agencies — would lose the ability to search Americans' communications without a warrant and lose several broad collection authorities. Data brokers would lose federal law enforcement agencies as customers for location, biometric, and browsing data. Tech companies would face court-supervised limits on government demands for technical assistance, though they gain protection from being conscripted under the broader ECSP definition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies, data brokers, surveillance-focused contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill extends Section 702 itself for four years, to April 20, 2030 — meaning the bulk collection of foreign communications, which incidentally sweeps in Americans' calls and emails, continues through 2030 rather than being allowed to expire or face a shorter, reviewable window [S2].

The warrant requirement applies to searching already-collected data, not to the collection itself; unevaluated information about Americans can still be held unless agencies determine it does not pertain to a covered person, and much collection of Americans' incidental communications remains lawful [S2].

National security agencies argue in good faith that warrant requirements slow foreign intelligence work; the bill responds with emergency exceptions — including warrantless access when there is an imminent threat of death or serious bodily harm — that agencies will press to use broadly, and agencies self-certify the factual basis for each emergency [S2].

The data broker ban binds only federal law enforcement directly; state and local police are covered by a reporting requirement rather than an outright prohibition, and the prohibition includes carve-outs for compilations, whistleblower programs, background checks, and "lawfully obtained public data" [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is explicit and stated in the bill: Americans get a warrant requirement for searches of their communications and a ban on buying their data from brokers, and in exchange the 702 program continues for four more years. The warrant and query limits have real exceptions and enforcement depends heavily on agencies auditing themselves, but the bill adds independent court experts, inspector general review, and data-retention limits that give the limits teeth beyond agency promises. On balance the privacy gains for ordinary people outweigh the operational cost to intelligence agencies, though critics on both sides have fair points — civil libertiers that 702 survives at all, and security agencies that warrants will slow urgent work.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill on March 12, 2026 and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2026 on March 12, 2026, joined by Sens. Mike Lee, Elizabeth Warren, and Cynthia Lummis as cosponsors [S2][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction; the only recorded action since is that referral [S4].

The bill's Judiciary referral matters because surveillance authority under FISA is typically shepherded by the Senate Intelligence Committee, and the bill's text is built around amending FISA and the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act [S1][S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything except time: because the bill has not moved, intelligence agencies keep their current warrantless query authority and data brokers keep selling to federal law enforcement. If it never advances, the agencies and brokers are better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and data brokers, for now

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors span both parties — two Democrats (Wyden, Warren) and two Republicans (Lee, Lummis) — with no recorded opposition in the chamber so far; the bill has not reached a vote, so no roll-call exists to score.

industries.note: The Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act section bans federal law enforcement from buying Americans' location, biometric, and web browsing data from brokers and from obtaining it through other agencies, with a public reporting requirement for state and local police purchases. Brokers currently sell this data to police without a warrant, which the bill treats as an end-run around the Fourth Amendment [S2].

industries.industry: National security agencies (FBI, NSA) and surveillance contractors
industries.note: Agencies would lose warrantless searches of the 702 database for Americans' communications, several broad FISA collection authorities, expanded data retention, and part of the expanded service-provider compulsion authority, and would face accuracy certifications and inspector general oversight. In exchange, the bill gives them a four-year extension of 702 to April 2030 [S2].

Providers would gain court oversight of government demands for technical assistance — the government must show a directive is necessary and narrowly tailored, and providers need not comply without a court order — and the repeal of the expanded electronic-communication-service-provider definition relieves smaller intermediaries from being conscripted. But providers remain the channel through which all this surveillance flows [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been parked in the Senate Judiciary Committee since its March 2026 introduction, with no hearing or markup. Surveillance reauthorization bills normally originate with the Intelligence Committees, which have historically resisted warrant requirements for 702 queries of Americans, so this bill is unlikely to advance unless it is folded into the debate over the next 702 reauthorization deadline in 2030. Most bills referred to committee never reach the floor, and this one faces that fate absent a reauthorization fight forcing the issue.
